newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn against Italy, Spain in EMU 1st wave-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Bonn against Italy, Spain in EMU 1st wave-analysts.

text.p: Bonn wants neither Italy nor Spain to join European monetary union (EMU) from the start because their membership would make it even harder to persuade Germans to give up the mark, economists said on Monday

While Spain has made more progress than Italy towards qualifying, the two countries will have the same trouble proving they can sustain the convergence they have achieved -- and Germany has recently been at the forefront of stressing the need for sustainability, the economists said.

The issue is a political minefield because Italy as a founder member of the EU would be loathe to accept a delayed entry if Spain were among the first to join at the scheduled 1999 launch date. That in turn worsens Spain's prospects.

"I don't see that Spain can leapfrog over Italy politically," said Alison Cottrell, an economist at PaineWebber in London who sees both Italy's and Spain's chances of being in the first wave of entrants as "very, very small."
"I take the line that if no Italy, then no Spain."

Despite Spain's insistence that its progress towards joining EMU is backed up by its economic data, Bonn is aware that millions of German voters who have holidayed in Spain in recent years are prejudiced by seeing the peseta in their pocket steadily lose value. The same is true of Italy.

"It's happening a little too fast for the average German citizen that these devaluation-endangered countries with higher inflation suddenly should become hard currency countries with low inflation," said Thomas Mayer at Goldman Sachs.

Opinion polls show a majority of Germans are unwilling to give up their tried and tested mark for an unknown quantity like the Euro. A poll published by "Stern" magazine in December showed 61 percent of Germans were now "fearful" of the euro, with only 16 percent "hopeful".
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl this week rejected the idea that Bonn was fundamentally opposed to Spain's EMU membership but declined to say if Spain should be admitted from the start.

Speaking to reporters on Thursday after talks with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar, Kohl made the non-committal statement that he was "watching with great interest and sympathy the enormous efforts made by the Spanish government."
His comments came just two days after a top German official said some countries which qualified for European Monetary Union (EMU) should stay outside for a time after 1999.
German finance ministry number two Juergen Stark made clear on Tuesday Bonn was worried some countries did not have the track record to show they could maintain economic stability after joining EMU.

He did not name any countries, but there was little doubt he meant southern European EU members like Spain and Italy when he said some countries which qualify on paper "would be well advised to maintain exchange rate flexibility for a certain period".
Economists agree it will be not be enough to assess countries on their performance in the key 1997 year.
"If you just go on the numbers for 1997 then you let in the crash dieters and the problem is that crash dieters don't keep the weight off, usually," said Cottrell.

German scepticism about Italy and Spain came to the fore again on Friday when Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber accused the Social Democrats (SPD) of wanting to water down the Maastricht criteria for joining EMU in 1999.

Accepting "creative accounting" to allow countries to join EMU meant that "we'll never succeed in having the Italians and the Spanish and the Portuguese (keep to) a strict application of the stability criteria," Stoiber said.
"Then the whole thing will start to slide and I don't think the population would accept getting a softer euro in place of our hard deutschemark," Stoiber told German television.
